content.content: Herein contains relevant information about the government and politics of the German republic.

options.title: Timeline of the Weimar Republic before 1928

content.content: The German Republic, called by some of our detractors as the "Weimar Republic", is a parliamentary republic with a somewhat weak president and a strong parliament, called the Reichstag. The Reichstag is responsible for governing, while the President has a largely ceremonial role but also has some important governing responsibilities.

The Reichstag is elected based on a proportional representation system, giving parties seats roughly proportional to their vote share in each electoral district. The Reichstag then elects the Chancellor and the cabinet by a majority vote, who are responsible for government. A majority vote-of-no-confidence can remove the current government.

The President is elected by a national direct vote, in two rounds. The second round is used if the first round does not result in a majority for one candidate; the candidate who receives a plurality in the second round becomes president. The role of the president is mostly to represent Germany, but the office also retains several crucial governing powers. The president may appoint a chancellor when no parliamentary majority has yet been established and may dissolve the Reichstag on the advice of the cabinet.
Germany is divided into a number of states, each of which have their own governments with some responsibilities. By far the largest and most important state is Prussia.

library_timeline.title: Timeline of the Weimar Republic before 1928

content.content: TIMELINE OF THE SPD AND THE REPUBLIC (UNTIL 1928)

content: : The SPD is formed as a merger of the General German Workers' Association, founded by Ferdinand Lassalle, and the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany, led by Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel. Eventually, the SPD grows to become the largest party in the German Empire.

: The Great War begins. The SPD votes in favor of war credits, with substantial internal dissent. This begins a policy of Burgfriedenspolitik, a general peace between all political parties and trade unions.
: The USPD, a left-wing anti-war split from the SPD, is formed.

: Following defeats in the war and uprisings by soldiers, sailors and workers, SPD leader Philipp Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic, and Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates. An armistice is declared, ending the Great War.

: The Spartacist uprising is defeated by the Social Democratic government. The Treaty of Versailles is signed under great protest from all political factions. The Weimar Constitution is signed and the first Weimar Coalition government is formed by the SPD, DDP and Centre parties.

: The Kapp Putsch is defeated by a general strike. This is followed by left-wing uprisings in the Ruhr, which are defeated by the Reichswehr and Freikorps. The Weimar Coalition loses its parliamentary majority.
: Communist uprisings in Saxony and Hamburg are defeated. Matthias Erzberger, the Centre politician associated with the armistice and fiscal reform, is assassinated.
: The Treaty of Rapallo normalises relations with the Soviet Union. Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau is assassinated. Most of the remaining USPD reunites with the SPD.
: Hyperinflation and the occupation of the Ruhr bring the Republic close to collapse. The currency is stabilised, passive resistance ends and extremist uprisings on both left and right are defeated.
: The Dawes settlement reduces the immediate reparations burden and opens a period of relative economic stability. Two Reichstag elections produce bourgeois-right governments.
: Friedrich Ebert dies. Paul von Hindenburg narrowly wins the presidential election. The Locarno treaties confirm Germany's western borders.
: A referendum on the expropriation of the former ruling houses fails. Germany enters the League of Nations.
: The SPD returns as the largest party. Hermann Müller's Grand Coalition begins the final parliamentary term covered by Social Democracy: An Alternate History.

content.content: Government status: caretaker cabinet pending the investiture of a new Chancellor.
Religion: 43% Protestant, 39% Catholic, 3% Jewish, 4% other faiths and 11% unaffiliated or undeclared.
Employment: 35% industrial and transport workers, 27% salaried and professional employees, 12% public service, 9% agriculture and forestry, and 17% other or retired.
The old confessional divide remains politically important, but urbanisation and inter-state migration have weakened the geographic monopolies of the CVP, BVP and Protestant conservative parties.
Prussia contains just under half of the population and remains the decisive arena in both Reichstag and presidential elections.

The Left Bloc and People's Bloc are electoral agreements rather than unitary parties. Each maintains common candidates in most constituencies, a joint parliamentary steering committee and a minimum programme. Neither has yet discovered a reliable method of making its component parties obey.
The election has now taken place. The final national vote was 53.2% for the People's Bloc and 46.8% for the Left Bloc.

content: Chancellor preference before polling day: Heinrich Windelen 38%, Hans-Jochen Vogel 34%, Burkhard Hirsch 9%, Oskar Lafontaine 7%, Alfred Dregger 5%, other or undecided 7%.

content.content: Most important issues: employment and industrial restructuring, 26%; pensions and social insurance, 20%; nuclear energy, 16%; federal finance, 13%; asylum and immigration, 11%; foreign affairs and defence, 8%; other, 6%.

The CVP is strongest among practising Catholics, small-town employees and organised Christian trade unionists. Its recent gains came principally from moderate RDP voters and pensioners who had supported the SPD in 1982.

The mass party militias of the Republic's crisis years no longer exist as legal organisations. The Reichsbanner was converted into a non-partisan civic defence association after 1946; the Stahlhelm was dissolved in 1952; and uniformed party formations are prohibited under the Associations Act.

The Federal Office for Constitutional Protection nevertheless estimates that several thousand people participate in violent revolutionary, national-revanchist or separatist groups. None possesses the membership, weapons or institutional protection enjoyed by the paramilitaries of the early Republic.

The DNVP maintains veterans' and frontier associations, while the LSPD has close relations with anti-nuclear direct-action networks. Both insist, with varying degrees of credibility, that these are not paramilitary organisations.

The fixed 600-seat Reichstag was introduced by the 1971 electoral reform. Seats are allocated proportionally within the states, with national adjustment seats used to restore overall proportionality.
The People's Bloc majority rests on eighteen seats. Either the DNVP or the combined BVP and regional lists can deprive it of a majority by withdrawing.
